episode_title: Undoing a $5 Billion Acquisition and Building a Durable Standalone Plaid (with Plaid CEO Zach Perret)

real_qa.q: Why did Plaid terminate the Visa acquisition deal for $5.3 billion?
real_qa.r: Plaid terminated the deal in January 2021 because the DOJ signaled they were going to sue to block the acquisition. While Zach Perret believed Plaid would have won the lawsuit, he estimated it would have taken two years to close the deal, which would have locked in a $5 billion price despite significant business growth and improved prospects. At that point, Perret believed Plaid was worth more independently, and many of the original concerns that had motivated selling were gone.
real_qa.requete: Plaid Visa acquisition termination reason DOJ

real_qa.q: How did Plaid's business perform during the pending Visa acquisition in 2020?
real_qa.r: Plaid's business boomed during the acquisition period. Consumers stuck at home realized they still needed financial services, driving heavy usage of Plaid's products. Money was free and startups were being founded everywhere—all of Plaid's customers got funded, crypto was taking off with many on-ramps, and neobanks were proliferating. This fintech boom created a great tailwind for growth, allowing Plaid to continue expanding rapidly despite the pending deal.
real_qa.requete: Plaid business growth 2020 Visa acquisition pending

real_qa.q: What was Plaid's valuation trajectory after walking away from the Visa deal?
real_qa.r: After terminating the Visa deal in January 2021 at $5 billion, Plaid raised the Altimeter round in April 2021 at approximately $13.5 billion valuation. A later fundraising round valued the company at $6 billion. Zach Perret was able to offer employees secondary sales at the higher $13.5 billion valuation, allowing them to take something off the table after the disappointing Visa deal cancellation.
real_qa.requete: Plaid valuation after Visa deal 2021 Altimeter

real_qa.q: How did Scott Cook's advice influence Zach Perret's decision on the Visa acquisition?
real_qa.r: Scott Cook, founder of Intuit, emailed Zach Perret the day after the Visa acquisition was announced, congratulating him but warning that if the acquisition failed, Perret would be fine and might actually be great. Cook shared that the best thing that happened to him was when Microsoft's acquisition of Intuit was blocked for antitrust, after which Intuit became a multi-hundred billion dollar company. This advice planted a seed in Perret's mind and proved prescient when he decided to walk away from the Visa deal.
real_qa.requete: Scott Cook Intuit Microsoft acquisition blocked antitrust

real_qa.q: What was Plaid's original business model before pivoting to the bank linking API?
real_qa.r: Plaid initially built consumer financial products including mobile budgeting tools and spending recommendations, similar to personal financial management tools. The company discovered that nobody wanted to use an app that told them to spend less money. After a conversation with the head of engineering at Venmo, who expressed interest in licensing Plaid's back-end infrastructure, the founders pivoted to focus exclusively on building an API for bank accounts rather than consumer-facing applications.
real_qa.requete: Plaid original business model consumer financial products pivot

real_qa.q: Were Plaid and Visa direct competitors in the payments market?
real_qa.r: Plaid and Visa were not direct competitors. While the DOJ alleged that Visa was a monopolist and that buying Plaid was a path to expand that monopoly, Zach Perret clarifies they did not compete on any specific product. Plaid was building an API for bank account linking and enabling new payment methods, while Visa was the historical credit card payment network. In a meta sense, you could say Plaid represented the new financial system competing against Visa's existing system, but they did not compete on individual products or transactions.

guest.bio_context: Zach Perret co-founded Plaid in 2012 with the thesis that banking and financial services were built for a world that had not envisioned the internet. He initially built consumer financial products before pivoting to focus on infrastructure—specifically creating an API for bank accounts. Under his leadership, Plaid negotiated to be acquired by Visa for $5.3 billion in January 2020, but terminated the deal in January 2021 after the U.S. Department of Justice filed an antitrust lawsuit to block it.
